_readme: Learn to prescribe: guided builder decisions, prescribing cases, and the effect of changing each variable. Verdicts: best, ok, avoid. An 'avoid' choice shows its feedback and asks the learner to choose again. 'set' changes the working prescription; 'order' is the line added to the order sheet. 'when' limits an option or step to a state (anticoag, citrateDilute, modality). All values are generic teaching values, not a local protocol.

bloodFlow.label: Blood flow (Qb)
bloodFlow.typical: 150–200 mL/min is common in adults. Dilute pre-filter citrate protocols often use 100–150 mL/min because the citrate volume rises with Qb. Above 250 mL/min depends on the access.

up.both: Plasma flow rises, so filtration fraction falls and the filter lasts longer. Small-solute clearance barely changes, because in CRRT clearance is limited by effluent flow, not blood flow. Access pressure becomes more negative and return pressure rises.
up.citrate: Citrate flow rises in proportion, because the citrate dose is set per litre of blood. Systemic citrate load and calcium losses rise. With a dilute citrate solution the extra volume also adds to effluent and pre-dilution, raising the delivered dose.
up.heparin: No change to heparin dosing. A higher Qb is one of the main tools for extending filter life, particularly with no anticoagulation.

down.both: Filtration fraction rises and the filter tends to clot sooner. Useful when the access cannot sustain a higher flow.
down.citrate: Citrate flow and citrate load fall. Lowering Qb is the main way to reduce the dose that a dilute citrate solution delivers on its own in a small patient.
down.heparin: Filtration fraction rises. Compensate by giving more replacement pre-filter or more of the dose as dialysate.

dialysate.label: Dialysate (Qd)
dialysate.typical: Often 1000–2000 mL/hr in CVVHDF, sized from the effluent target.

up.both: Effluent and small-solute dose rise with no effect on filtration fraction, because dialysate runs on the other side of the membrane and is not ultrafiltered from the blood. Losses of potassium, phosphate, magnesium and drugs rise.
up.citrate: More citrate-calcium complex is cleared into the effluent. Systemic citrate load falls (less alkalosis and accumulation risk), but calcium losses rise, so the calcium infusion may need to increase.
up.heparin: Only the dose and electrolyte effects above.

down.both: Dose falls unless replaced by another component of effluent.
down.citrate: Less citrate is cleared, so more reaches the patient. Watch for alkalosis and a rising total-to-ionised calcium ratio.
down.heparin: Only the dose and electrolyte effects above.

pre.label: Pre-filter replacement
pre.typical: Heparin or no anticoagulation: often about half of the replacement. Citrate: the citrate solution already dilutes the blood before the filter, so protocols usually give most replacement post-filter (this app uses 20% pre-filter).

up.both: Adds convective clearance, but dilutes the blood before the membrane, so each mL clears less than the same mL given post-filter. Compared with giving that volume post-filter, filtration fraction and haemoconcentration are lower and the filter lasts longer.
up.citrate: Adds to the pre-filter dilution the citrate solution already provides. Most citrate protocols keep it modest.
up.heparin: A key filter-life tool, especially with no anticoagulation or repeated clotting.

down.both: Each mL of effluent clears more, but moving that volume post-filter raises filtration fraction.
down.citrate: Little effect on the citrate itself.
down.heparin: Filter life may shorten if FF rises.

post.label: Post-filter replacement
post.typical: Sized so that filtration fraction stays under the protocol ceiling (25% in this app).

up.both: The most efficient convective clearance per mL, but it raises filtration fraction directly: blood leaving the filter becomes more concentrated and the filter clots sooner.
up.citrate: The main replacement route with citrate. Standard citrate protocols use calcium-free fluids and replace calcium separately.
up.heparin: Watch FF closely. Move some volume pre-filter or into dialysate if FF approaches the ceiling.

down.both: Filtration fraction falls. Dose falls unless the volume is given as dialysate or pre-filter replacement.

netUF.label: Net ultrafiltration
netUF.typical: 0–100 mL/hr when haemodynamics are fragile. When tolerated, many units aim for roughly 1–1.5 mL/kg/hr. Rates above about 1.75 mL/kg/hr have been associated with worse outcomes.

up.both: More fluid is removed. It counts toward effluent (dose) and filtration fraction. Removal faster than plasma refill causes hypotension.

down.both: Less fluid is removed and filtration fraction falls slightly.

citrateDose.label: Citrate dose
citrateDose.typical: 3–4 mmol per litre of blood, titrated to a post-filter ionised calcium of about 0.25–0.35 mmol/L using the local nomogram.

up.citrate: Post-filter ionised calcium falls (stronger circuit anticoagulation). Citrate flow, systemic citrate load and calcium losses rise. With a dilute solution the extra volume also raises effluent and pre-dilution.

down.citrate: Post-filter ionised calcium rises and the filter may clot sooner. Citrate load falls.

builder.title: Guided prescription builder
builder.stem: A 64-year-old man, 70 kg and 175 cm, has septic shock from pneumonia on norepinephrine 0.2 mcg/kg/min. He has been oliguric for 12 hours. Potassium is 6.5 mmol/L despite insulin-dextrose and calcium; pH 7.16, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L. He is about 6 L positive. No liver disease. Platelets 150, INR 1.3, no bleeding. Haematocrit 0.30.

decisions.title: Is CRRT indicated now?
decisions.teach: The timing trials (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI) showed no benefit from starting on AKI stage alone. Start when there is a trigger: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, diuretic-refractory fluid overload, uraemic complications or a dialysable poison. AKIKI 2 also showed that waiting beyond clear triggers offers no benefit.

options.label: Start now: refractory hyperkalaemia and severe metabolic acidosis are triggers
options.order: Indication: refractory hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis
options.feedback: Correct. Both are accepted triggers that have not responded to medical therapy.

options.label: Wait until creatinine rises further
options.feedback: Creatinine is not the trigger here. Potassium of 6.5 with a pH of 7.16 despite treatment needs renal replacement now.

options.label: Start because he is KDIGO stage 3
options.feedback: The decision is right but the reason is not. Stage alone is not an indication; the triggers are. Document the trigger.

decisions.title: CRRT, intermittent HD, or a hybrid (PIRRT/SLED)?
decisions.teach: Outcomes are similar across RRT types. KDIGO suggests CRRT for haemodynamically unstable patients and those with raised intracranial pressure, because slow continuous removal of fluid and solute is better tolerated. Intermittent HD lowers potassium fastest.

options.label: CRRT
options.feedback: Correct. He depends on norepinephrine, so continuous therapy is best tolerated.

options.label: Intermittent haemodialysis
options.feedback: Intermittent HD clears potassium fastest and can be used for a life-threatening level, but on vasopressors it risks intradialytic hypotension. If you choose it for the potassium, plan to move to CRRT.

options.label: PIRRT / SLED
options.feedback: A reasonable alternative where CRRT is limited, with slower removal than intermittent HD. This walkthrough continues with CRRT.

decisions.title: Vascular access
decisions.teach: KDIGO's order of preference is right internal jugular, then femoral, then left internal jugular, then subclavian on the dominant side last (subclavian lines risk stenosis that later rules out a fistula). Use ultrasound guidance. Choose the catheter length so the tip lies in the right atrium or at the cavo-atrial junction (commonly about 15 cm on the right IJ, 20 cm on the left IJ and 20–25 cm femoral). A tip that is too short causes recirculation.

options.label: Right internal jugular, ultrasound-guided
options.order: Access: right IJ dialysis catheter, ultrasound-guided, tip position confirmed
options.feedback: Correct. The shortest, straightest path with the most reliable flow.

options.label: Femoral
options.feedback: Acceptable and often quickest. Use a long enough catheter to reach the IVC, and expect flow problems with hip flexion.

options.label: Left subclavian
options.feedback: Subclavian access is last choice: it has the highest risk of central venous stenosis and harder flow.

decisions.title: Which CRRT modality?
decisions.teach: CVVH clears by convection (replacement fluid), CVVHD by diffusion (dialysate), and CVVHDF combines both. No trial shows a mortality difference between them. CVVHDF is a common default because the dialysate component delivers dose without raising filtration fraction. SCUF removes fluid only.

options.label: CVVHDF
options.feedback: Good default. Splitting the dose between dialysate and replacement keeps filtration fraction manageable.

options.label: CVVHD
options.feedback: Reasonable. Pure diffusion is kind to the filter; middle-molecule clearance is lower, which has not been shown to matter for outcomes.

options.label: CVVH
options.feedback: Reasonable, but the whole dose must cross the membrane as ultrafiltrate, so filtration fraction limits how much you can give. Watch the FF step.

options.label: SCUF
options.feedback: SCUF removes fluid only. It will not treat hyperkalaemia or acidosis.

decisions.title: Anticoagulation
decisions.teach: KDIGO suggests anticoagulation when there is no increased bleeding risk, and suggests regional citrate over heparin when citrate is not contraindicated. Citrate lasts longer per filter and causes less bleeding. Main cautions for citrate: severe liver failure or shock with poor lactate clearance (accumulation risk). Heparin is reasonable when citrate is unavailable or contraindicated, or when the patient already needs systemic anticoagulation.

options.label: Regional citrate
options.feedback: Correct. No liver failure, no contraindication, and his lactate is clearing.

options.label: Systemic unfractionated heparin
options.feedback: Reasonable if citrate is unavailable. It anticoagulates the patient as well as the circuit.

options.label: No anticoagulation
options.feedback: He has no bleeding risk. Without anticoagulation the filter will clot often, and each clot loses treatment time and blood.

decisions.title: Which citrate solution?
decisions.teach: Dilute citrate solutions (for example Regiocit or Prismocitrate, 18 mmol/L) run at about 10 times the blood flow in mL/hr and double as pre-filter replacement fluid. Concentrated solutions (ACD-A 113 mmol/L, 4% trisodium citrate 136 mmol/L) run at small volumes. ACD-A contains dextrose; 4% trisodium citrate carries a large sodium load. Use the product your unit stocks and the matching protocol.

options.label: Dilute: Regiocit 18 mmol/L
options.feedback: Good choice if stocked. Remember its volume counts toward effluent, pre-dilution and filtration fraction.

options.label: Concentrated: ACD-A 113 mmol/L
options.feedback: Good choice if stocked. Small volume, so it barely affects dose or FF.

decisions.title: Dose target
decisions.teach: Dose is expressed as effluent volume per kg per hour. RENAL (40 vs 25) and ATN (35 vs 20) showed no benefit from higher intensity. KDIGO recommends 20–25 mL/kg/hr delivered. Because of downtime and pre-dilution, the prescribed effluent must be higher than the delivered target.

options.label: 25 mL/kg/hr delivered
options.feedback: Correct: the upper end of the KDIGO range.

options.label: 20 mL/kg/hr delivered
options.feedback: Within the KDIGO range. With his potassium and acidosis many would aim for the upper end at the start.

options.label: 35–40 mL/kg/hr delivered
options.feedback: RENAL and ATN showed no benefit and more hypophosphataemia with higher intensity.

decisions.title: Expected downtime
decisions.teach: Filter changes, clotting, imaging and procedures stop treatment. A typical ICU loses about 10% of each day. Use your unit's observed downtime if you know it.

options.label: 10% (about 2.4 hours a day)
options.feedback: A sensible default.

options.label: 0%: the machine runs continuously
options.feedback: Downtime always happens. Assuming none guarantees underdosing.

options.label: 20%: frequent clotting and trips expected
options.feedback: Reasonable if your unit's data show this. Fixing the cause of the downtime is better than prescribing around it.

decisions.title: Blood flow (Qb)
decisions.teach: Blood flow sets plasma flow, which limits how much fluid can cross the membrane (filtration fraction). It barely changes small-solute clearance in CRRT. With citrate it also sets the citrate flow, because citrate is dosed per litre of blood.

options.label: 120 mL/min
options.feedback: Good for a dilute citrate solution: citrate runs at about 1200 mL/hr, leaving room for dialysate and replacement.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Acceptable. Citrate alone runs at 1500 mL/hr, most of his effluent target, so FF will be close to the ceiling.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: At 200 mL/min a dilute citrate solution runs at 2000 mL/hr, which alone exceeds his effluent target. Choose a lower Qb.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: A standard starting flow with concentrated citrate.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Fine if the access allows. Citrate flow and calcium needs rise with Qb.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Too low for this dose: filtration fraction will be high and the filter will clot.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Good. Higher Qb lowers filtration fraction and extends filter life.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Acceptable. Check FF, especially in CVVH.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Too low: filtration fraction will be high and the filter will clot.

decisions.title: Net ultrafiltration (fluid removal)
decisions.teach: Net UF is what leaves the patient. Set it from the fluid goal and what the circulation tolerates now, and reassess every few hours. He is 6 L positive but still on escalating norepinephrine.

options.label: 0 mL/hr (even balance) for now
options.feedback: Correct while vasopressor needs are rising. Start removing once he stabilises.

options.label: 50–100 mL/hr
options.order: Net UF: 50 mL/hr, stop if hypotensive
options.feedback: Reasonable if he is stabilising, with a clear hold parameter.

options.label: 250 mL/hr
options.feedback: About 3.6 mL/kg/hr in a patient on escalating vasopressors: likely to outpace plasma refill and cause hypotension.

decisions.title: Solutions
decisions.teach: Choose potassium, phosphate, calcium and buffer content deliberately. With citrate, dialysate and replacement are normally calcium-free and calcium is replaced by a separate infusion. Phosphate falls within 24–48 hours on phosphate-free fluids.

options.label: Potassium 0–2 mmol/L fluids for the first hours with potassium checks every 2–4 hours, then potassium 4
options.order: Solutions: K 0–2 initially, K checks 2–4-hourly, switch to K 4 when K < 5; phosphate plan from 24 h
options.feedback: Correct. Plan the switch before potassium overshoots low.

options.label: Potassium 4 fluids from the start
options.feedback: Safe but slower to correct a potassium of 6.5. Some units do this and rely on the volume of effluent.

options.label: Potassium 0 fluids for the whole run
options.feedback: Continuous potassium-free fluid causes hypokalaemia and arrhythmia risk once the level normalises.

monitoring: Electrolytes (Na, K, iCa, Mg, PO4) and a blood gas 6-hourly for the first day, then per protocol.
Citrate: post-filter iCa 1 hour after start and after each change, systemic iCa and total calcium to follow the ratio.
Heparin: aPTT or anti-Xa per the local nomogram; platelets daily for HIT.
Hourly fluid balance with a hold parameter for hypotension.
Check the delivered dose daily from the machine's effluent volume.
Review drug doses against a CRRT-specific reference.

cases.title: Septic Shock
cases.stem: 58F, 85 kg, 168 cm. Septic shock from cholangitis, source controlled. Norepinephrine 0.12 and weaning. Anuric. K 6.2, pH 7.19. Bilirubin 60, INR 1.4, lactate 2.8 and falling. Platelets 110. Hct 0.28. Unit uses Regiocit.

decisions.title: Anticoagulation
decisions.teach: Mild cholestasis with a falling lactate is not a contraindication to citrate. The concern is severe liver failure or shock with a rising lactate.

options.label: Regional citrate
options.feedback: No contraindication. Follow the calcium ratio given her liver tests.

options.label: Systemic heparin (bilirubin is up)
options.feedback: Works, but a bilirubin of 60 with a clearing lactate doesn't rule out citrate, and heparin gives shorter filter life and more bleeding.

options.label: None
options.feedback: No bleeding risk. You'd just be clotting filters.

decisions.title: Blood flow
decisions.teach: Effluent target ≈ 25 × 85 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 2400 mL/hr before pre-dilution. Regiocit ≈ 10 × Qb mL/hr.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Citrate 1500 mL/hr, leaving room for dialysate and replacement.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Citrate 2000 mL/hr: most of her effluent, a bigger citrate load and more calcium.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Low plasma flow for 85 kg, so FF runs high.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Good for filter life on heparin.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Fine. Check FF.

decisions.title: Net UF
decisions.teach: +4 L, pressor falling.

options.label: 0 mL/hr, reassess at 6 h
options.feedback: Reasonable while still on norepinephrine.
options.order: Net UF: 0 mL/hr, reassess at 6 h

options.label: 50 mL/hr, hold if MAP < 65
options.feedback: Also fine as she improves.
options.order: Net UF: 50 mL/hr, hold if MAP < 65

options.label: 200 mL/hr
options.feedback: Too fast on a pressor.

cases.debrief: Regiocit runs at about 10 × Qb, so at Qb 150 it is 1.5 L/hr of her effluent. That volume also drives pre-dilution and FF. If FF is over the ceiling, move post-filter replacement to dialysate: same dose, lower FF.

cases.title: Massive PE with AKI
cases.stem: 71M, 95 kg. Day 3 after massive PE, on therapeutic UFH. Oliguric AKI, pulmonary oedema despite furosemide. Off pressors. K 5.4, pH 7.29. Hct 0.36.

decisions.title: Circuit anticoagulation
decisions.teach: KDIGO: no extra circuit anticoagulation if the patient is already systemically anticoagulated.

options.label: Existing heparin infusion only
options.feedback: His heparin already covers the circuit.

options.label: Add regional citrate
options.feedback: Adds citrate and calcium monitoring for no benefit.

decisions.title: Modality
decisions.teach: Hct 0.36 means less plasma flow for any Qb, so FF climbs faster.

options.label: CVVHDF
options.feedback: Dialysate carries part of the dose without adding to FF.

options.label: CVVH
options.feedback: Possible, but at 95 kg with this Hct, FF will be the limit.

options.label: SCUF
options.feedback: He needs clearance too, not just fluid off.

decisions.title: Blood flow
decisions.teach: On heparin, pick Qb for filter life and what the line will run.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Suits his size and Hct.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Works, higher FF.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Too low for him.

decisions.title: Net UF
decisions.teach: Stable, oedematous. 1 mL/kg/hr ≈ 95 mL/hr.

options.label: 120 mL/hr, hold if MAP < 65
options.feedback: About 1.3 mL/kg/hr. Meaningful removal most patients tolerate.
options.order: Net UF: 120 mL/hr, hold if MAP < 65

options.label: 0 mL/hr
options.feedback: Safe, but fluid is one of the reasons you started.

options.label: 300 mL/hr
options.feedback: About 3 mL/kg/hr. Likely to outrun refill.

cases.debrief: No citrate means pre-dilution comes only from pre-filter replacement (50/50 split here). Net UF adds straight to effluent and FF. A high Hct lowers plasma flow, which is why Qb 200 and a dialysate component help.

cases.title: BMI 49
cases.stem: 49M, 150 kg, 175 cm. Septic AKI, K 6.1, fluid overloaded, off pressors. Unit uses ACD-A. Hct 0.32.

decisions.title: Dosing weight
decisions.teach: No validated rule: the dose trials had few very obese patients. Actual weight gives huge volumes; IBW under-doses. Adjusted weight (IBW + 0.4 × excess) is a common compromise.

options.label: Adjusted body weight
options.feedback: Reasonable. Recheck with labs and go up if clearance falls short.

options.label: Actual (150 kg)
options.feedback: Defensible, but you'll need over 4 L/hr of effluent.

options.label: Ideal body weight
options.feedback: Likely to under-dose.

decisions.title: Blood flow
decisions.teach: Big effluent needs plasma flow to keep FF down. ACD-A at 3 mmol/L ≈ 1.6 × Qb mL/hr.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Good if the line allows.

options.label: 250 mL/min
options.feedback: Needs good access. More citrate and calcium.

options.label: 120 mL/min
options.feedback: Not enough plasma flow for his effluent.

cases.debrief: Weight choice moves the effluent more than any other decision here. Write down the weight you used and judge adequacy from K, acid-base and urea over the first day.

cases.title: 40 kg
cases.stem: 82F, 40 kg, 150 cm. AKI after complicated colectomy. K 6.0, pH 7.22. Off pressors. Unit uses Regiocit. Target 22.5 mL/kg/hr delivered. Hct 0.25.

decisions.title: Blood flow
decisions.teach: Target ≈ 22.5 × 40 ÷ 0.9 = 1000 mL/hr before pre-dilution. Regiocit ≈ 10 × Qb.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Citrate ≈ 1000 mL/hr, close to her whole target, with a little left for dialysate and replacement.

options.label: 120 mL/min
options.feedback: Citrate alone roughly meets target. No dialysate or replacement needed; all clearance comes from the citrate.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Citrate alone gives about 27–28 mL/kg/hr. Drop Qb or switch to a concentrated citrate.

cases.debrief: Dilute citrate is part of the effluent, so it sets a minimum dose. In a small patient, choose Qb from the dose, or use a concentrated citrate.

cases.title: Liver failure, GI Bleed
cases.stem: 55M, 70 kg. Decompensated cirrhosis, active variceal bleed. Norepinephrine and vasopressin. Lactate 9 and rising, INR 2.8, platelets 40. AKI with K 6.4, pH 7.12. Hct 0.24.

decisions.title: Anticoagulation
decisions.teach: Citrate needs a liver to clear it. Cirrhosis plus shock with a rising lactate means high accumulation risk. Heparin is out with an active bleed.

options.label: None
options.feedback: Right for now. Lean on flow and pre-dilution and accept shorter filter life.
options.order: Anticoagulation: none (heparin-free prime per local practice)

options.label: Citrate, reduced dose
options.feedback: Some units do this with 6-hourly calcium ratios. With lactate 9 and rising, most would wait for shock to settle.

options.label: Systemic heparin
options.feedback: Active bleed, INR 2.8, platelets 40.

decisions.title: Modality
decisions.teach: With no anticoagulation, FF is your main lever on filter life.

options.label: CVVHDF
options.feedback: Dialysate carries dose without FF; pre-dilution protects the filter.

options.label: CVVHD
options.feedback: Also easy on the filter, but no pre-dilution.

options.label: CVVH
options.feedback: Whole dose crosses the membrane. Expect to push a lot of it pre-filter.

decisions.title: Blood flow
decisions.teach: Higher Qb lowers FF and shortens transit time through the circuit.

options.label: 200 mL/min
options.feedback: Best for filter life here.

options.label: 150 mL/min
options.feedback: Fine. Watch FF.

options.label: 100 mL/min
options.feedback: Slow flow and high FF will clot it fast.

cases.debrief: Without anticoagulation, prescribe for filter life: higher Qb, some dialysate, pre-filter replacement, low FF, few interruptions. Expect more downtime (15% used here) and check the delivered dose.
